transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Oh, thank you, doctor. Yes, I'll just set my purse right down here. It's very nice to meet you. I know it might seem a bit silly for someone my age to be coming in for something like this, but well, what brings me in is that for the past year or so, I just feel like I am always, always going. 

I’m constantly puttering around the house. Fixing things, arranging things. If I'm not reorganizing the pantry shelves—which I actually just completely emptied out and wiped down last Tuesday, mind you—I'm finding something else to tinker with. And it's not just at home, either. I keep volunteering for one more thing at the library or the church. They ask if anyone can help with the rummage sale, and before I know it, I'm organizing the whole clothing section and baking three dozen muffins. 

It’s just... well, even at 87 years old, when most people my age are perfectly content to just sit in their recliners and watch their afternoon programs or read a nice book, I have such a hard time just sitting down and being still. I’ll make myself a cup of tea, intending to just rest my feet, and two minutes later I'm up again because I remembered the guest room baseboards need dusting. My daughter tells me I'm going to wear myself out, and I suppose she's right, but I just can't seem to stop moving and doing. It's like I don't know how to just be quiet and sit anymore.
When you feel that urge to keep moving and doing things, what is typically going through your mind?

Oh, what is going through my mind? You know, that is a very good question, and honestly... I’m not entirely sure. It’s not like I’m sitting there having a full conversation with myself about it. 

I think my daughter, Susan—she’s the one who lives just two towns over, such a blessing to have her close—she asked me something very similar the other day when she caught me scrubbing the grout in the guest bathroom at seven in the morning. But the truth is, there really isn’t a specific thought at all. It’s not like I sit in my chair and think, "Oh, Margaret, you really must get up right this second and wipe down the ceiling fan." 

It’s more like... well, my mind is almost empty when it happens. Or maybe it's just that I don't even give myself the time to think before I'm already up and doing it. Like yesterday, I was watching Jeopardy—I do love Jeopardy, though it hasn't been quite the same since Alex passed, God rest his soul—and I didn’t consciously think about getting up. But before the first commercial break was even over, I found myself in the kitchen matching all the lids to the Tupperware. I didn't plan it. I didn't think about it. It’s more of a physical feeling, I suppose, like a little motor running inside me that just pushes me out of the chair. 

So, I suppose I don't really have a good answer for you. There really isn't much going through my mind at all, just this... this pull to be busy. Does that make any sense?
Looking back to when you were a child or teenager, were you also constantly on the go like this and having trouble sitting still?

Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, indeed. You know, it’s funny you should ask about that, because I was just talking to my sister Betty about this very thing last month. Betty is two years older than I am, and her memory is still sharp as a tack, bless her heart. 

But yes, even way back then, long before I was a teenager, I was exactly the same way. I remember being in grade school—this would have been at the old Roosevelt Elementary, which they tore down back in the seventies to build that shopping center that’s half empty now anyway—and I was constantly getting scolded by my teachers. Mrs. Gable, my third-grade teacher, she was a lovely woman but very strict, she used to get so frustrated with me. I was always popping right out of my seat. I just couldn't stay glued to the chair like the other children. 

And the talking! Oh, I was a talker. I still am, I suppose you've noticed! But back then, I would just blurt things out, talking right over my classmates when they were trying to answer a question. I just got so excited, you see, and the words would tumble out before I could stop them. I remember my mother coming home from parent-teacher conferences and sighing, telling my father that the teachers said I was "too lively." That was the polite way they put it back then, wasn't it? "Too lively." 

So, yes, it’s not a new thing at all. It’s been this way my whole life, this... this inability to just sit quietly and be still. Even as a little girl with pigtails, I was a handful, always buzzing around like a bee in a jar.
Do you also find it hard to keep your focus on tasks, or do you tend to get easily distracted and forgetful?

Focus? Oh, no, not at all. Once I start something, I am absolutely locked in. I mean, my goodness, just the other day when I was cleaning out that pantry I mentioned earlier, I started at about nine in the morning, right after my tea. And I didn't stop until almost two in the afternoon! I was pulling out every single can, checking the expiration dates—you wouldn't believe how long a can of water chestnuts can hide in the back corner, I think one expired in 2018!—and I wiped down every single shelf with that nice lemon-scented cleaner. I didn't get distracted once. I didn't even stop for lunch, which I know Susan would scold me for if she knew, but I was just so focused on getting it done perfectly. 

And forgetful? Heavens, no. My memory is still wonderful, thank the Lord. Like I said, my sister Betty and I, we remember everything. I can tell you the names of all my teachers from elementary school, I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation—it was a lovely pale yellow dress with a little white collar, very popular at the time—and I never forget an appointment or a birthday. I have five grandchildren and three great-grandchildren, and I send a card for every single birthday, always mailed exactly three days early so it arrives on time. So no, doctor, my mind is sharp and my focus is fine. It's just my body that won't seem to quit! I just don't have any trouble paying attention to what I'm doing, as long as I'm actually doing something.
